readings.title: The Story of My Life: the word at the well-house (chapter iv)
readings.challenge: Distinguish what the young child experienced from the meaning the adult writer gives it.
readings.focus: The day Anne Sullivan arrived and the morning at the pump when Keller understood that everything has a name.
readings.context: Helen Keller (1880–1968) became deaf and blind after an illness when she was nineteen months old. She wrote The Story of My Life (1903; this is the 1905 edition) while a student at Radcliffe College. In the previous chapter her family found, through Alexander Graham Bell and the Perkins Institution for the Blind in Boston, a teacher willing to come to their home in Alabama. Laura Bridgman was a deaf and blind woman educated at Perkins decades earlier. A sounding-line measures the depth of water under a ship; in the Bible, Aaron’s rod is a staff that blossomed. The [1] after the well-house paragraph marks an editor’s note pointing to Anne Sullivan’s own letter about this day, printed later in the book.
readings.contentNote: Keller describes weeks of anger and smashing a doll in a temper. She uses “dumb” in its older sense of “unable to speak.”

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter IV, the whole chapter; opens “THE most important day I remember in all my life is the one on which my teacher, Anne…”; closes “…over the joys it had brought me, and for the first time longed for a new day to come.”.

questions.prompt: Keller compares herself before her teacher came to a ship in fog. What did she lack, according to the comparison?
facilitatorNotes: The ship at least has a compass and a sounding-line to find its way; she had neither, no means of knowing where she was or how near help might be. The comparison turns a state she could not describe at the time into something a sighted, hearing reader can feel. Its last sentence calls her teacher “the light of love,” which joins teaching and affection.
evidence: I was like that ship before my education began, only I was without compass or sounding-line, and had no way of knowing how near the harbour was.

questions.prompt: Keller could spell “doll,” “pin” and “hat” weeks before the well-house. Why does she say she was not really spelling words yet?
facilitatorNotes: She copied the finger movements “in monkey-like imitation” without knowing that the movements stood for things or that words existed at all. What was missing was the idea of naming. She also could not tell “mug” from “water,” because she did not yet understand that each pattern belonged to one thing.
evidence: I did not know that I was spelling a word or even that words existed; I was simply making my fingers go in monkey-like imitation.
But my teacher had been with me several weeks before I understood that everything has a name.

questions.prompt: Compare how Keller feels about the broken doll before and after the well-house. What does she suggest about language and feeling, and how sure can the adult writer be?
facilitatorNotes: Before, she felt “neither sorrow nor regret,” only satisfaction; after, she gathers the pieces and feels “repentance and sorrow” for the first time. She suggests that words brought not only names but the ability to think about what she had done and to feel for others. She herself hedges (“if a wordless sensation may be called a thought”), so readers can ask whether the child truly felt no tenderness or simply had no way to know or express it.
evidence: Neither sorrow nor regret followed my passionate outburst.
for the first time I felt repentance and sorrow

readings.title: The Story of My Life: water, trees and the noisy city (chapter xxii, part 1 of 2)
readings.challenge: Separate what Keller perceives through touch, smell and motion from what she imagines or believes, and notice where her argument changes direction.
readings.focus: Rowing, canoeing and sailing, two tree friends, and a protest against the poverty of city streets.
readings.context: Helen Keller (1880–1968) became deaf and blind after an illness when she was nineteen months old; her teacher, Anne Sullivan, spelled words into her hand. She wrote The Story of My Life (1903; this is the 1905 edition) while a student at Radcliffe College, and the previous chapter was about the books she loves. Wrentham is a village in Massachusetts; Halifax is a harbour city in Nova Scotia, Canada, and Evangeline is Longfellow’s long poem set in Nova Scotia. A regatta is a series of boat races; men-of-war and gunboats are warships. King Philip was the English name for Metacom, a Wampanoag leader who fought the New England colonists in 1675–76; the tradition about the oak is one Keller reports. “Evidence of things unseen” echoes the Bible’s definition of faith (“the evidence of things not seen”), and “Give us this day our daily bread” is from the Lord’s Prayer. Capital and labour means employers and workers.
readings.contentNote: Keller describes poor city children and adults in harsh physical terms (“ugly, withered and cringing,” “gnarled and bent out of shape”) to protest their conditions; “Indian chief” is the usual phrase of her time.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter XXII, from the opening through her return to the country “after a year of work in town”; opens “I TRUST that my readers have not concluded from the preceding chapter on books that…”; closes “…not to think of all this when I return to the country after a year of work in town.”.

questions.prompt: Keller cannot see where her boat is going. How does she row and steer? List the senses she uses.
facilitatorNotes: Smell: she steers by the scent of water-grasses, lilies and bushes on the shore. Touch and pressure: the resistance of the water tells her when the oars are evenly poised and when she pulls against the current. Someone usually works the rudder, but sometimes she rows without it because steering by scent is “fun.” Ask what this shows about how much information a sighted rower ignores.
evidence: It is fun to try to steer by the scent of watergrasses and lilies, and of bushes that grow on the shore.
I know by the resistance of the water when the oars are evenly poised

questions.prompt: “I suppose you will smile when I say that I especially like it on moonlight nights.” Why does Keller expect her reader to smile, and how does she answer that smile?
facilitatorNotes: The reader assumes moonlight means nothing to someone who cannot see. She agrees she cannot see the moon climb, but says “I know she is there” and imagines feeling “the shimmer of her garments” in the water. She adds things she really feels: a fish, a pond-lily, the sudden warmth of open air. Readers can decide whether the moon is a fact for her, a fancy, or both; she herself says “I fancy.”
evidence: I cannot, it is true, see the moon climb up the sky behind the pines
I fancy that I feel the shimmer of her garments as she passes

questions.prompt: In the storm off Halifax, what words make the little sail-boat seem alive and brave? Why does Keller insist the passengers felt “excitement, not fear”?
facilitatorNotes: The boat “confronted the gale fearlessly,” “seemed to sit upon the wind,” swirls and springs; the waves howl and hiss. Giving the boat courage lets the passengers share it. Keller explains they trusted the skipper, who was “master of the situation.” Some readers may suspect a little bravado in “the hearts of vikings”; the applause from the warships suggests others thought the trip daring too.
evidence: Our little boat confronted the gale fearlessly
Our hearts beat fast, and our hands trembled with excitement, not fear

questions.prompt: Keller claims that everyone has “a sort of sixth sense–a soul-sense.” What does she mean, and what does she offer as evidence? Can such a claim be tested?
facilitatorNotes: She means an inherited, unconscious memory of the earth that lets people share experiences they have not had through eyes or ears. Her evidence is personal: Mr. Chamberlin taught her trees and flowers until she seemed to hear sap flow, and the quoted lines compare her to roots that share the tree-top’s sunshine. It is a belief offered as an image rather than a proof; readers can say whether the image persuades them and what a doubter would answer.
evidence: Each individual has a subconscious memory of the green earth and murmuring waters
This inherited capacity is a sort of sixth sense–a soul-sense which sees, hears, feels, all in one.

questions.prompt: Keller says the news of war and the struggles of “capital and labour” would “pass away,” yet she grows “hot and indignant” about the city’s poor. Does her proposed cure fit the problem she describes?
facilitatorNotes: She describes poverty as something forced on people: they are “condemned to live” in sunless tenements, with too little opportunity for their effort. Her cure is that men should leave the city for “simple, honest living.” Some readers will find this a sincere moral cry; others will notice that the poor cannot simply leave, and that the summer in Eden she enjoys is the very thing she says they lack. Both readings use her words.
evidence: But we little heeded these things.
while others are condemned to live in hideous, sunless tenements
Oh, would that men would leave the city, its splendour and its tumult and its gold, and return to wood and field and simple, honest living!

readings.title: The Story of My Life: games, statues and the stage (chapter xxii, part 2 of 2)
readings.challenge: Follow a list of pleasures closely enough to notice how each one is adapted to touch, and then weigh the very different final paragraph.
readings.focus: Bicycles, dogs, checkers, children, sculpture and actors, and the isolation the pleasures cannot remove.
readings.context: Recap: Keller has described rowing, canoeing on moonlit nights and a storm at sea; her tree friends at Wrentham; and her anger at the poverty of city streets, which she contrasts with the country. A tandem bicycle has two seats, one behind the other; “phiz” is slang for face; “dumb show” means acting something out without words. Diana and Venus are Roman goddesses (of the hunt and of love), shown in famous statues; bronzes are metal sculptures. Homer, the ancient Greek poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey, was said to be blind; Hellas is Greece. The three lines of verse are from John Milton’s Samson Agonistes, spoken by the blinded Samson; Milton was blind himself. Ellen Terry and Henry Irving were famous English actors. Joseph Jefferson was an American actor who played Rip Van Winkle for decades; Schneider (Rip’s dog) and Derrick belong to his stage version. The Rivals is an eighteenth-century comedy in which the timid Bob Acres is pushed into a duel. The 1905 printing reads “It there are children around,” a misprint for “If”; the text keeps the print.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter XXII, from “What a joy it is to feel the soft, springy earth” to the end of the chapter; opens “What a joy it is to feel the soft, springy earth under my feet once more, to follow…”; closes “…my sun, the music in others' ears my symphony, the smile on others' lips my happiness.”.

questions.prompt: How is Keller’s checkerboard made so that she can play by touch? How does she know when it is her turn?
facilitatorNotes: The squares are cut out so the pieces stand firm; black checkers are flat and white ones curved; a brass knob marks a king; white chessmen are larger than black. She feels the board after each move, and the jar of a piece shifting tells her when to play. Each change replaces sight with shape or vibration.
evidence: The black checkers are flat and the white ones curved on top.
The jar made by shifting the men from one hole to another tells me when it is my turn.

questions.prompt: When Keller misunderstands the children and does the wrong thing, “a burst of childish laughter greets my blunder.” Is the laughter unkind? What does the paragraph suggest about why she enjoys children?
facilitatorNotes: The laughter is part of the game: “the pantomime begins all over again,” and the hours leave them “good and happy.” Children lead her, show her things and act out what they mean when she cannot read their lips. They do not talk down to her; they simply try again. Some readers may still feel a sting in being laughed at; Keller presents it as shared fun.
evidence: A burst of childish laughter greets my blunder, and the pantomime begins all over again.
the wingéd hours depart and leave us good and happy

questions.prompt: Why does Keller follow her description of Homer’s face with three lines from Milton? What does Homer’s story give her?
facilitatorNotes: Milton, a blind poet, wrote the lines for blind Samson; Keller uses them for Homer, another blind poet, and her “how well I understand” joins herself to them. The chain shows that blindness and great poetry have gone together before. Homer’s song “won the blind poet an immortal crown”: his example suggests that a person living in darkness can still make something all ages admire, a hope a young writer might hold for herself.
evidence: Ah, how well I understand his deprivation–the perpetual night in which he dwelt–
it won the blind poet an immortal crown, the admiration of all ages

questions.prompt: Keller says she has “no sense whatever of dramatic action,” yet she “caught the drollery” of Bob Acres’s blunders. Is she contradicting herself?
facilitatorNotes: Not quite. She means she cannot invent the right gestures herself: when Jefferson asked her to suggest them she could only guess. But she can follow gestures someone else makes, through her hands, better than if the scene were spelled to her. Some readers will think she undersells herself, since her guesses were part of a real exchange with the actor.
evidence: I followed all his movements with my hands, and caught the drollery of his blunders and gestures in a way that would have been impossible had it all been spelled to me.
Of course, I have no sense whatever of dramatic action, and could make only random guesses

questions.prompt: After a chapter of pleasures, the last paragraph turns to “a sense of isolation.” Why end this way, and is “self-forgetfulness” a satisfying answer?
facilitatorNotes: The paragraph before claims her life “touches at many points the life of the World Beautiful”; the last admits a “shut gate” she cannot pass. Ending on both is more honest than ending on either. Her answer is to find joy in other people’s light, music and smiles. Some readers will find it generous and wise; others may feel she is asked, or asks herself, to swallow “bitter, futile words” too quietly. Either view should quote her.
evidence: Sometimes, it is true, a sense of isolation enfolds me like a cold mist as I sit alone and wait at life's shut gate.
So I try to make the light in others' eyes my sun, the music in others' ears my symphony, the smile on others' lips my happiness.

readings.title: The Story of My Life: hands and friends (chapter xxiii, part 1 of 2)
readings.challenge: Follow a writer who knows people through touch and smell, and test her general claims against her examples.
readings.focus: Keller describes what hands tell her, the faith Bishop Brooks gave her, and a poet’s tears.
readings.context: Helen Keller (1880–1968) became deaf and blind after an illness when she was nineteen months old; her teacher, Anne Sullivan, spelled words into her hand. She wrote The Story of My Life (1903; this is the 1905 edition) while a student at Radcliffe College, and this is the last chapter of her own account. Phillips Brooks was a Boston clergyman who became a bishop; Henry Drummond was a Scottish writer on religion; Swedenborg was an eighteenth-century Swedish writer on heaven and the spirit world. Oliver Wendell Holmes was an American poet; the Charles is the river at Boston. “Break, break, break” is a poem by Alfred Tennyson mourning a dead friend; “The Chambered Nautilus” is a poem by Holmes. A libation is a drink poured out as an offering.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIII, from “Would that I could enrich this sketch” to her visit to Oliver Wendell Holmes; opens “WOULD that I could enrich this sketch with the names of all those who have ministered to…”; closes “…After that I saw Dr. Holmes many times and learned to love the man as well as the poet.”.

questions.prompt: Keller says the hands of people she meets are “dumbly eloquent,” speaking without words. What can a handshake tell her? Find her two opposite comparisons.
facilitatorNotes: Some hands are cold and joyless, like “a northeast storm”; others “have sunbeams in them.” A child’s clinging hand gives her as much as “a loving glance” gives others. Touch does for her what faces and voices do for sighted, hearing people: it tells her what a person feels. (“Dumbly” here means without speech.)
evidence: it seemed as if I were shaking hands with a northeast storm
Others there are whose hands have sunbeams in them, so that their grasp warms my heart.

questions.prompt: Asked whether people bore her, Keller names the people she dislikes. Why does being “talked down” to exasperate her? Do you agree that it is a kind of hypocrisy?
facilitatorNotes: She compares it to someone shortening their steps to match yours: a pretence of equality that really points out the difference. She wants to be met as an equal mind. Some readers will argue that adjusting to another person can be kindness, not hypocrisy; Keller’s point is that it is insulting when it assumes she cannot keep up.
evidence: I also dislike people who try to talk down to my understanding.
They are like people who when walking with you try to shorten their steps to suit yours; the hypocrisy in both cases is equally exasperating.

questions.prompt: What was Bishop Brooks’s answer when the child Helen asked why there were so many religions? Why does she still prefer it after reading the Bible and works of philosophy?
facilitatorNotes: He said there is one universal religion, love: love of God and of “every child of God,” with good stronger than evil. He taught “no special creed or dogma.” After wider reading she found nothing “more soul-satisfying.” Readers with different beliefs, or none, can discuss whether one religion of love is possible, and whether Keller describes Brooks or her own faith.
evidence: There is one universal religion, Helen–the religion of love.
Bishop Brooks taught me no special creed or dogma
I have found no creed or system more soul-satisfying than Bishop Brooks's creed of love.

questions.prompt: In Holmes’s library, how does Keller know the room is full of books, and that he is crying? Why might the old poet have wept when she recited Tennyson?
facilitatorNotes: She smells print and leather and feels tears on her hand. She assumes she has distressed him. But Holmes was sitting by the fire “thinking … of other days,” and “Break, break, break” mourns a lost friend and time gone; he may have been moved by memory, or by the child herself reciting it. Keller does not explain, so readers must infer.
evidence: There was an odour of print and leather in the room which told me that it was full of books
I felt tears on my hand. I had made my beloved poet weep, and I was greatly distressed.
thinking, he said, of other days

readings.title: The Story of My Life: “my friends have made the story of my life” (chapter xxiii, part 2 of 2)
readings.challenge: Notice the ways friends find to reach a deaf-blind reader, and weigh the claim in the last sentence.
readings.focus: Whittier, Hale, Bell, the Huttons, Mark Twain and two friends she will not name.
readings.context: Recap: in the last chapter of her story, Keller describes the friends who shaped her life: hands that warmed or chilled her, Bishop Brooks and his “religion of love,” and Oliver Wendell Holmes weeping as she recited Tennyson. John Greenleaf Whittier, a Quaker poet, wrote “Laus Deo” (Latin for “Praise God”) to celebrate the abolition of slavery; Quakers said “thee” and “thy.” The [5] after Whittier’s “his” marks the book’s note giving what he wrote: “With great admiration of thy noble work in releasing from bondage the mind of thy dear pupil, I am truly thy friend.” In the Bible an angel frees the apostle Peter from prison. Alexander Graham Bell, inventor of the telephone, worked for the education of deaf children. Ascanius is the young son of the hero Aeneas in Virgil’s Aeneid. St. Nicholas was a magazine for young readers.
readings.contentNote: Whittier and Keller compare the freeing of a deaf-blind child’s mind with the freeing of enslaved people.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIII, from her visit to Whittier to the end of the chapter and of her own story; opens “One beautiful summer day, not long after my meeting with Dr. Holmes, Miss Sullivan and I…”; closes “…privileges, and enabled me to walk serene and happy in the shadow cast by my deprivation.”.

questions.prompt: Whittier gives Helen a statue and says of Anne Sullivan, “She is thy spiritual liberator.” How do the statue, “Laus Deo” and his inscription fit together? Is the comparison a fair one?
facilitatorNotes: “Laus Deo” celebrates the end of slavery, the statue shows fetters falling, and the inscription praises Sullivan for “releasing from bondage” Helen’s mind. Whittier sees one kind of freedom in another: language freed her from isolation. Readers may admire the comparison or question whether any condition should be likened to slavery; both deserve a hearing.
evidence: he placed in my hands a statue of a slave from whose crouching figure the fetters were falling
She is thy spiritual liberator.

questions.prompt: List the ways Keller’s friends find to “speak” to her or sign their names. What do these small inventions show about friendship?
facilitatorNotes: She reads Whittier’s and Mark Twain’s words by touching their lips; Gilder presses his mark deep into the paper; Hale pricks his signature in braille; she feels Twain’s humour in his handshake. Each friend changes a habit to reach her. Friendship here is shown in the effort to meet her where she is, which is the opposite of “talking down.”
evidence: read his answers by placing my fingers on his lips
he made his mark under his signature deep in the paper so that I could feel it
pricking his signature in braille
I feel the twinkle of his eye in his handshake.

questions.prompt: Keller helped Bell fly kites “by means of which he expects to discover the laws that shall govern the future air-ship.” What does this sentence tell you about when she was writing, and about Bell as a teacher?
facilitatorNotes: The flying machine is still a future thing: she was writing before people had flown in powered aircraft. Bell treats her as a helper in real experiments, and he “makes you feel that if you only had a little more time, you, too, might be an inventor.” Like Sullivan, he makes others feel capable.
evidence: helping him fly kites by means of which he expects to discover the laws that shall govern the future air-ship
He makes you feel that if you only had a little more time, you, too, might be an inventor.

questions.prompt: Why does Keller refuse to name some friends? Her last sentence says they “turned my limitations into beautiful privileges.” Do you accept that claim?
facilitatorNotes: Some things are “too sacred” for “cold print,” and the friend who pays for college does good “silent and unseen,” so naming him would undo his modesty. (Historians identify him as the industrialist Henry H. Rogers.) The last sentence gathers the chapter: her life is the work of her friends. But she also writes of the “shadow cast by my deprivation”: she does not deny the loss. Readers may find the ending generous or too serene.
evidence: things too sacred to set forth in cold print
Kind to every one, he goes about doing good, silent and unseen.
In a thousand ways they have turned my limitations into beautiful privileges, and enabled me to walk serene and happy in the shadow cast by my deprivation.
